rows.finding: Not a taxable category. IIT Law Art. 2 lists exactly nine income categories; converting CNY to USD is not among them. Taxes attach to the underlying income, not the exchange.

Comprehensive income taxed 3–45% progressive for residents; non-residents monthly/transaction basis (IIT Law Art. 2–3). Foreign-individual FX purchase for lawful income requires tax documents (S02 Art. 13), i.e. the income-tax trail is part of the transfer dossier.

Transfer-of-assets income is a taxable category at a flat 20% rate on income (IIT Law Art. 2(8), Art. 3(3)). Shanghai's official FAQ confirms tax must be settled and evidenced before FX purchase and remittance of the proceeds.
rows.amount_note: Gain computation and any local relief unverified (F05) — blank

rows.finding: Interest, dividends and bonuses taxed at a flat 20% (IIT Law Art. 3(3)); profit remittance needs the tax authority's filing form (S03 Section V).

Disposition of nonfunctional currency is a section 988 transaction; for an individual's personal transactions no gain is recognized from exchange-rate changes if the gain is USD 200 or less (§988(e)(2)). If the gain exceeds USD 200 the exclusion does not apply and the gain is ordinary income (§988(a)(1)(A)).
rows.amount_note: Gain above threshold = full amount, not excess only

rows.finding: U.S. citizens are taxed on worldwide income; amounts must be reported in USD using the prevailing rate at receipt/payment/accrual.

Required if aggregate foreign financial accounts exceeded USD 10,000 at any time in the calendar year. Due April 15, automatic extension to October 15. Whether the accounts produced income is irrelevant.
rows.amount_note: Filing duty, not a transfer cost

rows.finding: Thresholds: unmarried in the U.S. — USD 50,000 year-end / USD 75,000 anytime; married filing jointly in the U.S. — USD 100,000 / 150,000; unmarried abroad — USD 200,000 / 300,000; married filing jointly abroad — USD 400,000 / 600,000.
rows.amount_note: Filing duty, not a transfer cost

rows.finding: Non-willful violations up to USD 10,000 (statutory maximum, inflation-adjusted per 31 CFR 1010.821); willful violations up to the greater of USD 100,000 or 50 percent of account balances; criminal penalties may also apply.
rows.amount: up to $10,000 non-willful; greater of $100,000 or 50% of balances willful

rows.finding: Failure to disclose: up to USD 10,000, plus USD 10,000 per 30 days of continued non-filing after IRS notice, to a potential maximum of USD 60,000; criminal penalties may also apply.
Chinese income tax paid on the same income generally qualifies for a credit (or deduction) via Form 1116; the credit is the main tool to avoid double taxation of the underlying income.
rows.amount_note: Depends on tax actually paid (F01/F05) — blank

rows.item: FX-rule violations (structuring, quota lending, false documents)
rows.finding: Prohibited by S01 Art. 7 and S08. Underground banking and money laundering are named enforcement targets (S08). The Implementing Rules' default fine clause (Art. 39) was repealed by Huifa [2023] No. 8 (F10); enforcement now runs through the Foreign Exchange Administration Regulations and criminal law.
rows.amount_note: Current fine schedule not re-fetched — blank

rows.finding: Fiat-crypto exchange and related services are illegal financial activities strictly banned (PBOC Yin Fa [2021] No. 237); offshore exchanges serving domestic residents are likewise illegal.

rows.item: Bottom line on 'tax penalties' for moving your own money
rows.finding: Neither jurisdiction taxes the conversion itself for personal transactions (China: not a taxable category; U.S.: §988(e) personal exclusion). The 'considerable tax' usually feared is (a) Chinese income tax on the underlying earnings if unpaid, (b) U.S. tax on unreported income or §988 gains, and (c) FBAR/8938 filing penalties. All three are avoided by documentation and filing, not by finding an untaxed channel.
